title: Wayfinding in Interior Environments: An Integrative Review
review_question: To review and synthesize the published literature on wayfinding in interior environments.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Studies were included if they focused wholly or in part on wayfinding, were conducted in interior environments, were empirical, and written in English. Studies were excluded if subjects were children, visually impaired, physically or mentally disabled, or if they focused on technology testing.

synthesis_conclusions: Wayfinding is a complex phenomenon involving multiple cognitive processes and behaviors.

User factors (wayfinding cognition, wayfinding behavior, individual and group differences) and environmental factors (environmental elements, environmental cues) are broad factors influencing wayfinding.
Spatial memories are the most studied cognitive function related to wayfinding, and their acquisition can improve performance, though different levels of spatial memories have varying effects.
Spatial working memory plays a critical role in spatial knowledge acquisition.
Different brain regions are responsible for different types of spatial knowledge (e.g., hippocampus for survey, caudate nucleus for route).
There is an association between survey knowledge acquisition and path integration.
Anxiety (neophobia) affects navigation patterns, with people tending to stay closer to maze borders in early learning phases.
Aging negatively affects spatial memories and spatial abilities, leading to less effective place learning and reduced wayfinding performance.

Sex differences exist in spatial memory acquisition and strategy use; men often outperform women in survey knowledge tasks, while women tend to rely on landmark-biased strategies and report less confidence.
Older adults tend to rely more on egocentric reference frames, while men prefer allocentric frames.
Path integration yields more accurate spatial updating than piloting when moving between regions.
Different levels of information (e.g., route vs. survey descriptions) produce different levels of behavioral performance, with route descriptions leading to fewer errors.
Older adults prefer more salient environmental information, and sex differences are evident in information pick-up (women prefer landmark cues, men prefer geometry cues).
People with good self-reported navigation ability have different neuroanatomy and are faster wayfinders with fewer errors.
Visuospatial working memory is important for fast wayfinding.
Floor plan complexity (e.g., ICD) negatively affects cognitive map accuracy and wayfinding performance (time, wrong turns, backtracking).
Geometrical attributes (e.g., misalignment, clipped corners, oblique intersections) influence survey knowledge acquisition and navigation time.
Volumetric survey knowledge can be acquired in multilevel buildings with visual connections like atriums.
Environmental legibility (high global and local) is associated with shorter paths.
Higher step depth to goal values are associated with lower completion speeds and longer paths.

Unfamiliarity leads to navigation in areas with higher local topological properties and use of central point heuristic; familiarity leads to navigation in areas with higher global topological properties and use of floor heuristic.
People use more integrated spaces when uncertain and tend to use routes central to the building as a whole in multilevel structures.
Integration of spatial knowledge acquired from separate regions is possible with verbal descriptions.
Local geometric cues of edges are used for spatial learning, but non-geometrical cues can compete.
People prefer paths that minimize energy expenditure, have longer lines of sight, and are wider and brighter.
Warm corridors are more memorable, cool corridors more navigable, and bright corridors are perceived more positively.
In emergency situations, people tend to follow brighter and wider corridors (at T-type intersections), but may not necessarily follow signs, relying on environmental affordances.
T-type intersections influence path preference, and in emergency egress, people may tend to turn left (cultural influence).
Landmarks with visual detail and combined auditory/visual information improve spatial memories, but tracking multiple landmarks increases processing load during spatial updating.
Prior knowledge is important for inferring logical associations between landmarks and targets.
Neural mechanisms distinguish useful from misleading landmarks, and landmarks generally improve wayfinding performance.
Signage is more effective than YAH maps, but does not compensate for floor-plan complexity issues.
Signs with pictograms, human figures, and high color contrast improve comprehensibility, which is also influenced by education, age, and culture.
Signs with both words and icons lead to shortest completion times and distances.
Signs reduce emergency egress time, but in emergencies, people may prioritize doors or environmental affordances over exit signs.
Learning from maps can be effective, but maps can be time-consuming and negatively impact performance, especially if misaligned or overly detailed.
Schematic maps can yield better performance than highly detailed ones.

Environmental factors like signs, architectural features, maps, interior elements, logical clusters, pairings of elements, structural elements, and furniture are used as sources of wayfinding information.
Background knowledge helps infer logical associations when spatial knowledge is insufficient.
evidence_gaps: Environmental factors such as regions, edges, and nodes have not been studied as extensively.
The effects of environmental factors on other cognitive functions, such as spatial reference frames and spatial updating, have been neglected.
More exploratory studies are needed to identify other environmental factors and attributes that might impact wayfinding.
Additional studies are needed into people's background knowledge and logical associations regarding built environments.
limitations: Only four databases were searched, potentially missing relevant studies.
The search was limited by the keywords used, potentially missing relevant articles due to interchangeable terminology (e.g., wayfinding and navigation).
Studies published after the initial search (November 2017 - December 2018) were not included.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Individuals form internal mental representations (cognitive maps) of their environment to aid navigation and spatial understanding.
Wayfinding performance is influenced by the acquisition and integration of different types of spatial knowledge: landmark, route, and survey knowledge.
The design and clarity of environmental features (e.g., paths, edges, districts, nodes, landmarks) contribute to an environment's legibility, which facilitates wayfinding.

mechanism_chain.description: The review synthesizes mechanisms by which environmental design features influence cognitive processes of spatial knowledge acquisition and updating, ultimately affecting wayfinding behavior.
